title: Gratitude for joy
hookLine: Marcus Aurelius opens his private notebook with a whole book of thank-yous, person by person
tomorrow: Seneca blamed his manager for some dying trees. who planted them?

cards: Thank-you notes have a reputation as a chore your relatives make you do after birthdays. A Roman emperor wrote them anyway, to himself. Marcus Aurelius kept a notebook, the book we call the Meditations.
And before he writes a single rule for his own life, he writes a list of people and what each one gave him.
The very first line, in George Long's translation: "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper."

teach.b: Then his mother: reverence, generosity, and a simple way of living, far from the habits of the rich.
A teacher named Rusticus: for lending him the discourses of Epictetus from his own collection. On it goes, person by person, a whole first book of debts.
It ends by thanking the gods for good grandparents, good parents, good teachers, good friends.
That's the Stoic practice at the front door of the Meditations: before you work on yourself, name what you were given, and by whom. Marcus didn't think he made himself.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: an emperor's private book starts with pages of thank-yous. And notice what he thanks people for. Not riches or rank, mostly.

Good things: a temper learned, a book shared, a way of living watched up close. That's gratitude for joy: going back to the person behind a happy thing and naming exactly what it gave you. Not "thanks for everything."
From you, I learned this. From you, I got that. It closes the circle on a week of joy: savored, shared, feasted, laughed at, let fly, and now thanked.

how: The first book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations is a list of thanks: person by person, what each taught or gave him. Stoic practice on a personal path often borrows the form: from this person, I received this.

o: thanking someone by name for a specific happy thing
repaying a favor right away so you owe nothing
feeling lucky in general about how your life turned out

games.q: Marcus's first book: tap the pairs.
p: good morals and a governed temper
generosity and a simple way of living
lent him the discourses of Epictetus

s: the Meditations open with a list of thank-yous
the first book names person after person and what each gave him.
Marcus credits Rusticus with sharing Epictetus
Marcus writes that he made himself who he is
he does the reverse: he names who and what he owes.

games.q: at your grandpa's retirement party, everyone says "thanks for everything." you're asked to say a few words. what would Marcus do?
o: name one specific thing he gave you: from you, I learned this.
list his achievements, so everyone knows how much he did.
keep it general, so nobody feels left out.
games.why: Marcus's first book thanks each person for a specific gift: a temper, a book, a way of living.

practice: Write one line by hand in the shape of Marcus's first book: from this person, I received this one good thing. A second line, if one comes. Then sit with their faces for the rest of the time, and send the line later if you like.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude for joy: thanking the person behind a happy thing, by name, for exactly what they gave, as Marcus did.

carryVoice: Your line: thank you. Said to a name, for the one specific thing they gave. Talk tomorrow.
